extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetic style/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative criteria for writing and judging poetry (diction, metre, originality, revision), as discussed in a work of literary criticism. Emphasizes natural diction, editorial discipline, and the mental faculties that produce poetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic logic: reason for every word and position
rubrics_metrics.description: In the truly great poets there is a reason assignable, not only for every word, but for the position of every word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge recounts his master’s exercises (using Didymus’s synonyms) to show that synonyms are not interchangeable; the choice and placement of each word must be justified by sense and effect. Anti-pattern: casual synonym-swapping or careless phrasing that ignores particular fitness of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of hackneyed poetic imagery and stock phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain well-known poetic tropes and words (e.g., lute, harp, lyre, Muse, Pegasus, Parnassus, Pierian spring) are to be avoided as abominations in precise poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge relays his master’s mockery of such phrases and gives examples (the repetitive Alexander and Clytus simile, manchineel fruit) as overused, ill-fitting ornaments. Anti-pattern: relying on ready-made poetical ornaments that recur across subjects; these weaken individuality and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double epithets and excessive ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess of ornament (such as newly coined double epithets) and turgid, swelling diction are faults—especially common in youthful composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge admits critics’ charges of obscurity and profusion of double epithets, and describes pruning such excesses in later editions. Example anti-patterns: juvenile poems with 'strained and elaborate diction' or 'swell and glitter' that obscure thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for austere, natural diction
rubrics_metrics.description: An austerer and more natural style is superior; natural thoughts require natural diction and plainness where force and dignity allow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge reports deliberately studying to impress ease and simplicity on later work; he praises poets (Bowles, Cowper) who combine natural thought with natural diction. Guidance to writers: cultivate simplicity and resist floridness except where justified by subject and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returnability: enduring-pleasure test for essential poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Not the poem which we have read, but that to which we return with the greatest pleasure, possesses the genuine power and claims the name of essential poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge frames this as a primary criterion of poetic value: true poetry yields a continuous undercurrent of feeling and repeated enjoyment rather than a one-off astonishment. Anti-pattern: works that excite only transient surprise or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translatability is a vice in diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever lines can be translated into other words of the same language without diminution of significance, association, or worthy feeling are, so far, vicious in their diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge excludes pleasure from mere novelty as a 'worthy feeling.' The test: if substitution or paraphrase leaves the line essentially the same, the diction lacks essential poetic density. Example anti-pattern: lines that read as paraphrasable prose clothed in poetic trappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid translating prose-thoughts into poetic language
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic modern defect is treating 'poetic' diction as merely a translation of prose thoughts into verse-language, producing artificial and arbitrary phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge traces this tendency (partly to Latin-versing schooling) where poets prepare prose thought then pick line-fragments to dress it—resulting in 'thoughts translated into the language of poetry.' Anti-pattern: poetry that feels like dressed-up prose or 'translations of prose thoughts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of feeling and intellect (reconcile heart and head)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poetry reconciles heart and head: it combines natural thoughts with natural diction and unites feeling with reasoned expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge praises poets (e.g., Cowper, Bowles) who first combined natural thought with natural diction, 'reconciling the heart with the head.' Evaluate poetry by how well it balances emotional power and intellectual clarity rather than sacrificing one to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre imposes necessary consequences on diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of metrical composition is essentially different from that of prose; metre’s origin and elements constrain diction and condition the metrical writer’s choice of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge defends lines that run into one another (versus end-stopped couplets) by appealing to classical metres and the logic of poetic rhythm. Guidance: choose diction compatible with metrical demands rather than forcing prose syntax into verse form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid novelty and self-admiration for their own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude from poetic worth the pleasure derived from mere novelty in the reader and the author's desire to excite wonderment at his own cleverness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge criticizes fashions (e.g., certain French tragedies) where each line seems to celebrate the author's cleverness—'hieroglyphics' of self-admiration. Anti-pattern: ostentatious verbal tricks that prioritize authorial display over integrated feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three characteristic sins of youth to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Three sins likely to beset a young writer: (1) doleful egotism and recurrence of favourite phrases, (2) low creeping language disguised as simplicity, (3) indiscriminate use of elaborate and swelling language and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge himself satirized these in early sonnets (Nehemiah Higginbottom). Writers should beware of these temptations and practice self-scrutiny; examples in his own juvenilia illustrate each fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous editorial discipline and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistent, strict revision—refusing repeated faults, rewriting exercises until faults are cured—is an imitable and valuable method in forming taste and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge recounts his schoolmaster’s practice of accumulating exercises, pointing out repeated faults, tearing up work with two similar faults, and requiring rewrites. Guidance to writers: apply severe revision habits; prune phrases and restructure until faults are eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects appropriate to poetic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong choice of subject (e.g., forcing abstract or metaphysical truths into poetic form) can cause faulty diction; some subjects demand restraint and simpler diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge observes that his own earlier defects partly originated in trying to give poetic colouring to abstract metaphysical truths. Advice: match subject matter to a mode of diction that can naturally carry its emotional and intellectual weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporary models to form taste but with discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The productions of contemporary genius often have the most vivid effect on youthful minds and can shape taste strongly; this influence should be used with critical judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge describes how Bowles’s sonnets rescued him from unprofitable metaphysical preoccupations and inspired natural diction. Guidance: read living poets to form sensibility but evaluate them against principles (truth, nature, logic) rather than imitate blindly.
